title: The protocol for AI-generated code: read it, explain it, find the questionable choice, replace one part, test it every time
story:
Generation has made producing a large amount of plausible code almost free. The temptation that follows is obvious: paste it, run it, and if nothing throws, ship it. That path is fast in exactly the way that matters least.

The reason it fails is not that generated code is bad. Much of it is better than what a hurried person writes. The reason is that it is produced from what code usually looks like, not from what this system is responsible for — and those diverge precisely where the interesting decisions are. So the flaws are not random: they cluster in the places where the right answer depends on context the generator did not have. A call with an argument that used to be correct. A query that behaves fine on a development dataset and not on a production one. An absent timeout. A check that should have happened before the action and did not.

Every one of those runs correctly on first execution. That is the part worth internalising, because it defeats the only test the paste-and-run approach applies. The absence of a crash is not evidence of anything except the absence of a crash.

So the protocol is a sequence of five things, and the order is not decoration.

Read every line before it goes in. Not after, because after it is in, you are reviewing your own work and will read what you expect to see.

Explain each block in words. The reason this step exists is that the sensation of understanding code and the ability to explain it are different things, and only the second one is testable. Any block you cannot narrate is a block you have not read, however carefully your eyes moved.

Find the questionable choice, on the assumption that there is one. This is the step people skip, and the assumption is what makes it work: looking for a specific number of problems finds them, while looking for problems in general finds none and feels thorough. An unhandled empty case, a nested loop over the same collection twice, a missing bound.

Replace at least one part yourself. Not to improve it — to establish that you can. Ownership is the ability to change something, and the moment a block is untouchable you have taken on a dependency rather than written code.

Then write a test and run it. Not a check that it works, which is what running it already showed, but a test of the behaviour you claim it has at the boundaries where the generator had no context.

Underneath all five is one criterion, and it is the thing to keep if the steps are forgotten. The question is not whether the code works. It is whether you could have written it, and whether you can now say why it is the way it is. A system nobody on the team can explain is unmaintainable regardless of who or what produced it — and generation makes it possible to reach that state far faster than typing ever did, without anything visible going wrong on the way.

The honest cost is that this is slower than pasting, and the comparison people make is against the wrong baseline. It is not slower than writing the code by hand. It is slower than not reviewing, which was never a real option for code that was going to be maintained.

problem.move: Read before pasting, explain each block aloud, look for a definite number of questionable choices rather than for problems in general, replace at least one part to establish you can, and test the boundaries the generator had no context for. The criterion underneath: could you have written it, and can you say why it is this way?
problem.invariant: Generated code is produced from what code usually looks like, not from what this system is responsible for, so its flaws cluster where the right answer depends on context the generator did not have — and those flaws run correctly on first execution.
problem.breaks: The protocol assumes a reviewer competent to recognise the questionable choice. Applied by someone who cannot, it produces the ceremony without the review and a stronger false confidence than pasting would have, because five steps were performed. It is a discipline for people who could have written the code, not a substitute for being able to.

cost.time: a review pass on every generated block, which is the whole of the saving in the cases where the code was fine
cost.beats: pasting and running, which is faster and tests only for crashes, and writing it by hand, which is slower than both and produces code somebody understands by construction

worked.problem: What is wrong with pasting generated code that runs correctly, and what would you do instead?
worked.reasoning:
The problem is that running correctly is the one property the failure mode does not violate, so the only check being applied cannot detect it.

Generated code is produced from what code usually looks like rather than from what this system is responsible for, and those diverge exactly where the interesting decisions are. So the flaws are not randomly distributed; they cluster in the places where the right answer depended on context the generator did not have. An argument that used to be correct. A query that is fine on a development dataset and collapses on a production one. A missing timeout. An authorisation check that should have preceded the action.

Every one of those executes without error the first time. The absence of a crash is evidence of the absence of a crash and nothing else, which is why paste-and-run is not a weak process but an empty one for this class of defect.

What I would do instead is five steps, in order, and the order matters.

Read every line before pasting rather than after — after it is in, you are reviewing your own work, and you will read what you expect to see.

Explain each block in words. The reason this step exists is that the feeling of understanding code and the ability to explain it are different, and only the second is testable. A block you cannot narrate is one you have not read, however carefully you looked at it.

Find the questionable choice, assuming there is one. This is the step that gets skipped and the assumption is what makes it work: looking for a specific number of problems finds them, while looking for problems in general finds none and feels rigorous.

Replace at least one part — not to improve it, but to establish that you can. Ownership is the ability to change something, and a block that has become untouchable is a dependency rather than code you wrote.

Then test the boundaries the generator had no context for, which is different from checking that it works, since running it already showed that.

The criterion underneath all five is the thing to keep if the steps are forgotten: not whether the code works, but whether you could have written it and can say why it is the way it is. A system nobody can explain is unmaintainable whatever produced it, and generation makes that state reachable much faster than typing did, with nothing visible going wrong on the way.

I would name the limit too, because this protocol can be performed rather than done. It assumes a reviewer competent to recognise the questionable choice. Someone who cannot gets the ceremony without the review — and ends up more confident than they would have been from pasting, because five steps were completed. It is a discipline for people who could have written the code, not a replacement for being able to.

And the cost should be compared to the right baseline. This is slower than pasting. It is not slower than writing the code by hand, and pasting without review was never a real option for code that was going to be maintained.

problem.practice: Take the last generated block you accepted and try to explain each part of it out loud without re-reading. Wherever you stall is code you have shipped and do not own.

beats.broke: Generated code is produced from what code usually looks like rather than what this system is responsible for, so its flaws sit exactly where context was missing — and all of them run correctly the first time.
beats.fix: Read before pasting, explain every block in words, hunt a definite questionable choice rather than problems in general, replace one part to prove you can, and test the boundaries the generator could not know about.
beats.cost: A review pass on everything, which is the entire saving in the cases where the code was fine — and the protocol can be performed without being done by anyone unable to recognise the questionable choice.
